Introduction

People have always wondered whether, as well as hearing sound, we could somehow “see” it, and so understand it better. In centuries past, this was perhaps mainly a concern of royalty and the wealthy, because sound was bound up with the music and instruments they loved. Today it matters far beyond the entertainment of the upper classes; it touches every corner of social life. Where there are people, there is sound; and where there is sound, there is a jianghu, as the Chinese martial-arts saying goes: a world of heroes and villains, where good and evil are clearly drawn. “Good” sounds, such as music, should be brought out at their very best; “bad” sounds, such as noise, should be wiped out without a trace. Visualizing sound helps on both fronts. As Sun Tzu put it, know your enemy and know yourself, and you can fight a hundred battles without peril.

I’m covering sound visualization in two parts. This one is about early sound imaging, in two sections:

  1. Visualizing vibration

  2. Visualizing sound waves

Part 2 will introduce modern and contemporary imaging techniques such as beamforming, acoustic holography and Scan&Paint, which are used very widely in industry today.

1. Visualizing vibration

As I mentioned in an earlier article, Pythagoras was the first to study how the pitch of a string relates to its length. But sound imaging as such began in the 18th century, in 1787 to be precise, when Ernst Chladni first “saw” a plate vibrate. Many of you have probably seen the video below, which works on the same principle as Chladni’s experiment. Patterns like the one on the cover, which reveal a plate’s vibration modes, are called Chladni patterns. Draw a violin bow across the edge of a steel plate and it excites the plate’s modes, and fine sand on the surface traces out the nodal lines perfectly. Chladni patterns were so captivating that even Napoleon was fascinated by them and had Chladni’s Die Akustik (Acoustics) translated into French.

Chladni patterns in action

Video source: [https://stevemould.com/]

In 1827, Charles Wheatstone (of Wheatstone bridge fame) first proposed the idea of a “microphone.” But his microphone was not the device we know today. It was based on the kaleidophone, an instrument that also visualized the vibration patterns on the surface of a vibrating body, not sound waves.

Forty years later, our old friend the big boss, Helmholtz, made another grand entrance, refusing to be left out. He invented the vibration microscope to observe the vibrations of violin strings and of human speech. That is how, in the 19th century, people finally learned how a string actually moves when a bow is drawn across it.

Helmholtz motion on a violin string [http://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/Bows.html]

Over the following decades, August Kundt (yes, the Kundt’s tube used to measure impedance is named after him) visualized standing waves in a tube, and the British physicist John Tyndall (as in the Tyndall effect; small world…) observed wave phenomena through the propagation of light.

The next man’s masterpiece made me swear out loud: holy crap, a Fourier transform done with fire! This genius was Rudolph Koenig, and his invention was the manometric flame. Here’s how it works:

Sound is picked up by a tube and makes a membrane vibrate (think of how a modern microphone works). The vibrating membrane makes the supply of fuel gas in the pipe vary periodically, so the flame flickers with almost the same period as the membrane. There are many such membranes, of different sizes, which split the sound into frequency bands. On the right is a rotating mirror in which you can watch the flames change with the sound: sound visualization, mission accomplished! Combined with the more precise Helmholtz resonator, this was the oscilloscope of its day, performing a Fourier transform on sound directly! The second half of the video below shows the manometric flame plus Helmholtz resonators in all their glory. The beauty of mechanics and physics, right before your eyes: welcome to science up close.

And now, over to Master Wang for a demonstration, with plenty of oil (a joke on the catchphrase of Wang Gang, a popular Chinese cooking vlogger)

2. Visualizing sound waves

Between 1859 and 1864, August Toepler invented schlieren photography, which uses light to “photograph” the propagation of sound waves. It was the first time in the history of acoustics that the propagation of a wave had been made visible. This major discovery, or invention, inspired many scientists to run similar experiments, even in other fields, as in the schlieren images that reveal supersonic shock waves.

One of the scientists it inspired was Ernst Mach (sound familiar?). By visualizing sparks with the latest imaging technology of the day, which could measure the propagation speed of waves precisely, he was the first to show that a spark produces not only sound waves but also supersonic shock waves (er… that sounds super weird. Or is it super-sound weird?). So the M in

should be clear now, right?

Next, a moving object will challenge a sound wave three times:

“Slower than you!” | Subsonic, M < 1

“As fast as you!” | Transonic, M = 1

These three GIFs are from the ISVR [Institute of Sound and Vibration Research], University of Southampton

Note that subsonic and supersonic, the first and third cases, should not be confused with infrasound (f < 20 Hz) and ultrasound (f > 20 kHz); in Chinese, the terms are easy to mix up. The former describe speed, the latter frequency.

Remember the father of architectural acoustics from our first lesson? If you’ve forgotten, write the lesson out 50 times as punishment:

A history of acoustics: architectural acoustics

Highlight these 19th-century greats and write them down in your notebook: they were all polymaths and turn up everywhere.

Building on the work of those before him, Sabine, the father of architectural acoustics, was the first to visualize how sound travels in a concert hall. He set off sparks in the hall to generate weak shock waves (still sounds weird) traveling at very nearly the speed of sound, and imaged them with the shadowgraph technique. At last, people could excitedly “see” the sound they heard in a concert hall. The set of images below shows sound striking all sorts of poses in different concert halls:

Afterword

This installment looked back at the history of sound visualization and, once again, marveled at the ingenuity and persistence of those who came before us. The next one may interest you more: it covers beamforming, acoustic holography and Scan&Paint, techniques in wide use today, from the traditional auto industry to emerging fields such as speech recognition and virtual reality.

I’m about to go home for Chinese New Year, so the next installment will be out in two weeks. Stay tuned.

Happy Year of the Pig, everyone!

(Written 2019-01-29)
